passage:
Madhuri: Ok, before we argue: everyone write ten topic ideas on paper. No talking. 10 min ⏱️
Sachin: Even wild ones?
Madhuri: Especially wild ones. Then we read them all out, no comments
Sachin: Done. 10. One is "bus-delay predictor" 😅
Kirti: Mine: plant disease from leaf photos, library seat finder, exam timetable clash checker...
Madhuri: Great. Now score each 1-5 on: can we finish it, do we care, will our guide approve
Sachin: Wait, I'd never have said mine out loud in a group
Madhuri: That's why paper first 🙂 Pool the scores tonight?
Sachin: Yes. Bus predictor got 4 from me on interest but 2 on feasibility, fair.
Kirti: Leaf photos top so far. Guide meeting on Monday?
Madhuri: Booked.

qa.q: How many topic ideas did each person write?
qa.a: Each person wrote ten topic ideas.

qa.q: What is Sachin feeling about sharing an idea aloud?
qa.a: Sachin feels shy: Sachin says the idea would never have been said out loud in a group, and the paper step allows sharing anyway.

qa.q: What alternative approach could work if the scores end in a tie, and why?
qa.a: They could run a small test of the top two ideas with the guide, because a tie means the scoring cannot separate them and outside input can.

qa.q: How does Kirti experience the process?
qa.a: Kirti reads the ideas from paper and sees the leaf-photo idea come out on top, so the scoring gives Kirti a fair say next to louder voices.

grounding: Shows divergent brainstorming on paper followed by scored voting on feasibility, interest and guide approval so quieter members are heard.

passage: In the engineering college outside Hassan, the project room had a slow ceiling fan and one working plug point. Harish, usually the loudest in any group, surprised everyone. "This time, no talking for ten minutes. Everyone writes ideas alone. At least two each." Rekha, who hardly spoke in meetings, wrote four. When they pinned all ten on the soft board, hers included a moisture monitor for coffee drying yards near her village and an app to track milk collection at the local dairy. Then they scored each idea from one to five on three things: can we build it, do we care about it, and will Professor Gowda approve. The milk-collection idea came first, with top scores in the first two columns. Rekha went red. "I didn't think anyone would pick mine." Harish grinned. "Nobody picked it. The numbers did."

qa.q: How many ideas did Rekha write?
How did Rekha feel when her idea came first?
qa.a: Rekha felt shy and surprised, going red because she never expected her idea to be chosen.

qa.q: What else could keep quieter members heard later in the project?
qa.a: The team could keep writing silently before discussing at key decisions, like choosing features, not only at the start.

qa.q: How does Harish see the silent writing?
qa.a: Harish, usually the loudest, sees it as a way to let everyone contribute, and credits the scores rather than taking the credit.

grounding: Shows a team writing ten topic ideas silently, pooling them, and scoring each on feasibility, interest and guide approval, giving quieter members a fair say.

passage: In a borrowed tutorial room at the university in Lagos, Chidi handed out sticky notes. "Five minutes. Write project ideas. Don't show anyone yet." Sami, who had barely spoken in their first two meetings, filled three notes before anyone else finished one. When the ten notes went up on the wall, one of Sami's read: "Offline app for market traders to track stock without data." Ada had written "drone delivery", which she admitted was mostly for fun. They scored every idea from one to five on how buildable it was, how much they cared, and whether their supervisor would approve. Drone delivery got a five for interest and a one for buildability. Sami's market app got fours across the board and came out on top. Sami smiled at the table, then looked up. "I nearly didn't write that one," Sami said. "It felt too small."

qa.q: What did Sami's top idea say?
qa.a: Offline app for market traders to track stock without data.

qa.q: How did Sami feel about the winning idea before the vote?
qa.a: Sami felt unsure, almost not writing it down because it seemed too small.

qa.q: What else could the team do now that Sami's idea is chosen?
qa.a: They could talk to a few market traders early, to check the problem is real and shape the app around what they need.

qa.q: How might Ada see her drone idea losing?
qa.a: Ada seems relaxed about it, having written it mostly for fun, and the scores made the loss feel fair.

grounding: Illustrates a team gathering ten ideas silently and scoring them on feasibility, interest and supervisor approval, which lets a quiet member's idea win.
